title: Super-Resolution in the Right Latent Space: A Frozen Vision-Foundation Substrate

paper.title: Super-Resolution in the Right Latent Space: A Frozen Vision-Foundation Substrate
paper.abstract:
Abstract In an image latent space, the embeddings of high-resolution, natural, and sharp images form a manifold. Degradation of high-resolution images pushes their embeddings off this manifold. Real-world super-resolution (SR) then becomes the task of mapping the degraded embedding back onto this manifold: not anywhere on the manifold, but to the point that preserves what the input still carries, both its semantics and pixel details. Every published method implements this mapping in a reconstruction-oriented latent space or pixel space. We claim these spaces are the wrong substrates for SR. Low-resolution and degraded images are embedded far from the manifold, making the mapping difficult and expensive. The lack of semantic information in these substrates also makes it difficult to navigate to the faithful point on the manifold, causing severe hallucination when degradation is heavy. Thus, restoring in a suitable latent space is crucial
to the SR task. We show that the latent space of 23 23 fused layers of a frozen DINOv3-L is one such space that makes the SR task easier. Degraded images are embedded near the manifold. Moreover, this substrate contains a hierarchy of information, from pixel record to degradation-robust semantics, directly guiding the model to find the faithful point on the manifold. On this substrate, a 415 415 M decoder is trained under reconstruction and adversarial objectives to map the degraded embeddings back and decode to pixel space in one pass. The resulting model, RAESR, attains the best fidelity–perception trade-off among state-of-the-art adversarial and diffusion-based restorers on RealSR, DRealSR, LSDIR and DIV2K-Val, at 37 37 ms per 512 × 512 512{\times}512 image on a single H20 GPU. Swapping the substrate for a VAE latent under an identical recipe loses on
every metric.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: In an image latent space, the embeddings of clean, sharp, natural images form a manifold. Degradation pushes an image’s embedding off this manifold, and real-world SR is the task of mapping it back onto the correct point on the manifold, the point that stays faithful to the input in both semantics and surviving detail. Choosing the suitable latent space as the substrate for this task is therefore crucial. A suitable space should offer two properties. First, degraded images should be embedded near the manifold, so that the map back is easier and cheaper. Second, the space should carry a rich hierarchy of information to directly guide the map to the faithful point. High-level semantics tell the model which details are correct to synthesise, and low-level pixel information tells it which details must be preserved and what is noise to be removed. Current real-world SR methods restore in spaces with neither property. They either restore in the pixel space itself ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) , or in the latent of a variational autoencoder ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Wu et al., 2024b ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024a ) . Since these spaces are reconstruction-oriented, they faithfully preserve the degradation. As a result, degraded images are embedded far from the manifold (Fig. 1 a). The map to the manifold is therefore hard and expensive by default, and the lack of semantic information makes it even harder to navigate to the faithful point on the manifold. Lightweight GAN restorers in these spaces usually miss the manifold. Other methods make the distant map possible by training or adopting a visual generative prior such as diffusion, and pay with huge model size and slow inference. Even then, the long and weakly guided map can land on the manifold away from the faithful point, creating hallucinations (Fig. 1 a). Mitigations have been tried: fine-tuning the encoder to close the distance between degraded and clean embeddings ( Chen et al., 2025b ) , and injecting extra semantic guidance, from a text encoder ( Wu et al., 2024b ; Yu et al., 2024 ) or from the features of a vision foundation model ( Wu et al., 2026 ; Jangid et al., 2025 ) . However, these never solve the problem itself. We believe SR must be conducted in a suitable latent space to be efficient, and we claim that the averaged layers of the DINOv3-L encoder form such a latent space (§ 3.1 ). DINOv3 ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) is a self-supervised vision transformer trained on 1.7 1.7 billion curated, unlabelled images by self-distillation. Its network learns to match its own representations across augmented views of the same image, rather than to reconstruct pixels. As a result, degraded images are encoded close to the manifold (Fig. 1 b). The decoded images along the straight interpolation line between the degraded and the clean embedding show this directly (Fig. 1 , strips). In this latent space the decodes turn clear and natural much earlier than in the SD3-VAE latent (§ 5.1 ). Moreover, the fusion preserves a hierarchy of information, from a near-lossless pixel record in the shallow layers to degradation-robust semantics in the deep layers, which provides direct guidance for the map to the faithful point (§ 3.1 ). Therefore, the one-step map is much easier to learn, as shown in Fig. 1 b. Figure 1: The choice of latent space decides the task. (a) A reconstruction-oriented latent. (b) The fused DINOv3-L latent (ours). Strips: decoded images along the straight latent line z α = ( 1 − α ) ​ z LR + α ​ z HR z_{\alpha}=(1-\alpha)\,z_{\mathrm{LR}}+\alpha\,z_{\mathrm{HR}} in each space. RAESR is built on this substrate. One pass of this single trained 415 415 M decoder maps the degraded embedding back and decodes it to pixels. Averaged over four benchmarks, RAESR is first among the twelve published methods we evaluate on NIQE, MANIQA and DISTS and second on MUSIQ, LPIPS and TOPIQ (Table 1 ). It attains the best fidelity–perception trade-off and the best efficiency–perception trade-off (Fig. 2 ), at 719 719 M inference parameters and 37 37 ms per image on one H20. Figure 2: Perceptual-Fidelity and Perceptual-Efficiency tradeoffs. Circle area scales with inference parameter count. The vertical axis fuses the six perceptual metrics, each min–max normalized and re-oriented, then averaged with equal weight. (a) against LPIPS; (b) against measured latency (one H20, batch 1 1 ). Construction and robustness checks of the fused score: App. B.4 .

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: (i) We build RAESR, an efficient one-pass restorer that attains the state-of-the-art fidelity–perception and efficiency–perception trade-offs among the twelve published methods we evaluate, at 37 37 ms per image, with a distilled variant at 30 30 ms (§ 4 , App. G ). (ii) We redirect future SR research toward choosing a suitable latent substrate for the task. (iii) We characterize what makes a substrate suitable. Degraded images should be embedded near the manifold. All levels of information should be present in the substrate as direct guidance to the faithful point (§ 1 ). (iv) We rigorously analyze why the fused latent of DINOv3-L is such a space (§ 3.1 , § 5 ).

sections.heading: Restoring in a reconstruction-oriented space.
sections.text: Every line of real-world SR operates in such a space. Since these spaces offer neither of the two aforementioned properties, each family pays its own price. The one-pass adversarial restorers Real-ESRGAN ( Wang et al., 2021 ) , BSRGAN ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) and Real-HAT-GAN ( Chen et al., 2023 ) perform the map directly in one step, with no generative prior or external guidance. They are small and fast, but they fall short of the manifold and outputs are blurry. The diffusion line makes the long map feasible with a pretrained text-to-image prior. StableSR ( Wang et al., 2024a ) , DiffBIR ( Lin et al., 2024 ) , SeeSR ( Wu et al., 2024b ) , PASD ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , SUPIR ( Yu et al., 2024 ) and DiT4SR ( Duan et al., 2025 ) sample it over tens of steps, at billions of parameters and seconds per image (Table 1 ). OSEDiff ( Wu et al., 2024a ) , PiSA-SR ( Sun et al., 2025 ) , TSD-SR ( Dong et al., 2025 ) and AdcSR ( Chen et al., 2025a ) distil the schedule to one step but keep the backbone, while ResShift ( Yue et al., 2023 ) and SinSR ( Wang et al., 2024b ) train a short chain from scratch. None of them changes substrate, so the map stays long and weakly guided.

sections.heading: Working around the two defects.
sections.text: There have also been attempts to mitigate the two defects of the reconstruction-oriented latent space. Against the distance, FaithDiff ( Chen et al., 2025b ) fine-tunes the VAE encoder jointly with the prior to close the gap between degraded and clean latents. DiffBIR ( Lin et al., 2024 ) restores in pixel space before generating. Against the missing direct guidance, StableSR ( Wang et al., 2024a ) trains a time-aware encoder to condition the frozen prior, SeeSR ( Wu et al., 2024b ) conditions on tags from a degradation-aware extractor, PASD ( Yang et al., 2024 ) adds a captioner and pixel-aware cross-attention, SUPIR ( Yu et al., 2024 ) scales to large-scale text annotation, and, nearest to this work, VOSR ( Wu et al., 2026 ) and F2IDiff ( Jangid et al., 2025 ) condition the generator on DINOv2 features. Every remedy still preserves the reconstruction-oriented substrate. We take the opposite route and change the substrate.

sections.heading: Representation autoencoders.
sections.text: RAE ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) and RAEv2 ( Singh et al., 2026 ) show that a frozen self-supervised encoder with a trained decoder can replace the VAE for diffusion transformers, and RAEv2 introduces the multi-layer fusion our latent adopts (§ 3.1 ). That line is developed for generation and clean reconstruction. We carry the substrate to restoration.

sections.heading: 3.2 One decoder pass
sections.text: Because the degraded images are encoded near the manifold and the latent carries a rich hierarchy of information, the mapping back is short and well-guided. Thus, a single medium-sized decoder suffices to make it and to decode to the pixel space in one pass. Let x LR x_{\mathrm{LR}} be a degraded and low-resolution observation of a high-resolution image x HR x_{\mathrm{HR}} . We place the entire restoration burden on a trainable decoder G θ G_{\theta} over the frozen substrate: x ^ HR = G θ ​ ( E ⁡ ( U ​ p ​ s ​ a ​ m ​ p ​ l ​ e ​ ( x LR ) ) ) , \hat{x}_{\mathrm{HR}}\;=\;G_{\theta}\!\left(E(Upsample(x_{\mathrm{LR}}))\right), (2) where Upsample denotes the bicubic upsampling operation to the same dimension as x HR x_{\mathrm{HR}} . There is no sampling loop and no iterative refinement. After the decoder we align each output channel’s mean to the input’s, which avoids any colour shift and is a free improvement at almost no cost (App. B ). The decoder G θ G_{\theta} embeds the latent with a linear map d → 1152 d\to 1152 , applies 28 28 transformer layers ( 16 16 heads, MLP width 4096 4096 , 2D RoPE ( Su et al., 2024 ) ) over the token grid, and predicts 16 2 × 3 16^{2}{\times}3 pixels per token before unpatchifying, with a total of 415 415 M parameters.

sections.heading: 3.3 Training objectives
sections.text: The decoder must map onto the manifold, at the point faithful to the input. It must reproduce what survived the degradation and synthesise what the degradation destroyed in the right details. The loss emphasizes both tasks. The encoder is frozen throughout, in each stage, only G θ G_{\theta} was trained to minimize ℒ = ℒ 1 + λ p ​ ℒ LPIPS + λ adv ​ ℒ adv , \mathcal{L}\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{1}\;+\;\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LPIPS}}\;+\;\lambda_{\mathrm{adv}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adv}}, (3) with λ p = 1.0 \lambda_{\mathrm{p}}\!=\!1.0 (VGG16 LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) ) and λ adv = 0.5 \lambda_{\mathrm{adv}}\!=\!0.5 wherever the adversarial term is active. Both ℒ 1 \mathcal{L}_{1} and LPIPS only supervise faithfulness and cannot map the embedding back onto the manifold. Where details are destroyed, the reference is one completion among many valid ones, and a loss that regresses to the reference optimizes to the average of those completions, which is blur ( Blau & Michaeli, 2018 ) . The adversarial term supplies what regression cannot. It accepts any completion whose texture is real rather than pulling toward the mean, and so pushes the embedding onto the manifold. It is also the part of the loss that needs the most care (§ 3.4 ). Training proceeds in three stages. Stage 1 starts from the official RAEv2 ViT-XL reconstruction decoder ( Singh et al., 2026 ) , replaces its original positional embedding with 2D RoPE, and trains without the adversarial term on bicubically downsampled 512 512 px LSDIR images. Stage 2 applies strong second-order Real-ESRGAN degradation ( Wang et al., 2021 ) at 512 512 px, and trains with the critic active. Stage 3 aligns training with deployment. It is a short finish under a mixture of strong, medium and mild degradations. App. I documents data, schedules and every hyper-parameter.

sections.heading: 3.4 Adversarial training
sections.text: The adversarial term is what guides the learning of the map back onto the manifold. Thus, we need a critic that can provide rich and direct guidance. It needs the same hierarchy of information to decide whether a synthesised region is right for the image at each level, from low-level texture statistics to high-level semantics. Following the projected discriminators of Sauer et al. (2021) and the off-the-shelf critics of Kumari et al. (2022) , we therefore build it on the same representation family the substrate is built from (Fig. 4 ). The restored image and its ground truth pass through a frozen DINOv3-B encoder, and each of its 12 12 layers is read by its own trainable convolutional head, which emits one logit per token as the “realness” of that token in that particular information level. The heads carry 191 191 M learnable parameters in total and are discarded after training. Reading every layer through its own head is the critic-side counterpart of fusing every layer into z z . Realism is judged at every level, from texture statistics to the plausibility of semantics. Two properties of this design, both visible in Fig. 4 , make that realism requirement fine-grained and relative. First, the judgment is dense . No logit is pooled into an image-level score, so every region is judged on its own and a weak region cannot be averaged away by the rest. Second, it is paired by position . The logit of the restoration at position p p is compared with the logit of the ground truth at the same position of the same image, never with a batch statistic. The bar at each position is therefore the realism the reference itself attains there. Where the reference is smooth the bar is low, so the term does not ask for texture the scene does not have. Where the reference is detailed the bar is high, and the requirement is stricter. Figure 4: The critic. sections.heading: 4.1 Protocol
sections.text: We evaluate 4 × 4\times real-world SR on four benchmarks: RealSR ( Cai et al., 2019 ) ( 100 100 images), DRealSR ( Wei et al., 2020 ) ( 93 93 ), LSDIR ( Li et al., 2023 ) ( 250 250 ) and DIV2K-Val ( Agustsson & Timofte, 2017 ) (3000). None of them is seen in training. We compare twelve public methods (Table 1 ) that fall into three categories: adversarial restorers, diffusion models trained from scratch, and diffusion models built on a text-to-image basis. Every row is computed with the official checkpoint at official defaults. No method trains against any reported metric (App. B ). The cost columns of Table 1 are measured on one NVIDIA H20 at batch 1 1 on the 128 × 128 → 512 × 512 128{\times}128\rightarrow 512{\times}512 task. Latency is the mean of 30 30 CUDA-event measurements after 8 8 warm-up iterations, memory is the peak GPU allocation reported by PyTorch over the timed run, and parameters count every module on the timed path. Every method runs its official repository unmodified at native precision. We report nine metrics, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, NIQE, MUSIQ, MANIQA, TOPIQ and CLIP-IQA ( Zhang et al., 2018 ; Ding et al., 2022 ; Mittal et al., 2013 ; Ke et al., 2021 ; Yang et al., 2022 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) , averaged over the four benchmarks.

RAESR achieves the best scores among all twelve published methods on NIQE, DISTS and MANIQA , and the second-best on LPIPS, MUSIQ and TOPIQ. Following the perception–distortion framework of Blau & Michaeli (2018) , we divide the nine metrics into two families. PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS are fidelity metrics and measure the discrepancy between the output and its reference. DISTS, NIQE, MUSIQ, MANIQA, TOPIQ and CLIP-IQA are perceptual metrics and rate the perceived quality of the output as an image in its own right. Within the fidelity family we place the most weight on LPIPS, which is calibrated on human judgments of which of two images is closer to the reference ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) . PSNR and SSIM instead reward exact pixel agreement, and the degradation has made exact agreement impossible. The estimator that maximises PSNR is the blurred posterior mean rather than any sharp image ( Blau & Michaeli, 2018 ; Ledig et al., 2017 ) . Under this classification RAESR attains the best fidelity–perception trade-off in the table. It is second on LPIPS, narrowly behind TSD-SR, first on three of the six perceptual metrics with a clear margin on NIQE, and second on two more. RAESR also attains the best trade-off between inference cost and performance (Fig. 2 ). It runs 719 719 M inference parameters, 37.2 37.2 ms and 1.57 1.57 GiB per image; RAESR-Distilled lowers all three to 502 502 M, 30.0 30.0 ms and 1.18 1.18 GiB. In Table 1 only the four smallest baselines carry fewer parameters, and none of them is close in quality. Only Real-ESRGAN is faster, and it trails on every perceptual metric. RAESR is 1.6 × 1.6\times faster than the fastest one-step diffusion baseline (AdcSR) and 59 59 – 514 × 514\times faster than the 20 20 – 50 50 -step methods, while TSD-SR, the nearest competitor, is 3.1 × 3.1\times larger and 2.8 × 2.8\times slower. Fig. 5 shows the qualitative results. The GAN restorers work in pixel space, where the map is too hard, and thus fall short of the manifold. Their reconstructions are blurred in every sample. The diffusion baselines pay for the map but still land at the wrong point on the manifold, which shows up as hallucination or as a loss of the original semantics. In the boat image, RAESR is the only model that reconstructs the canopy in the background and renders the pole and everything around it cleanly. In the second image, it is the only model that preserves the building in the background. It is also the only model that preserves the real physics of the fox’s nose, recreating the fur that sweeps over it in the correct direction. RAESR-Distilled replaces the frozen DINOv3-L encoder with a distilled frontend and reuses the released decoder unchanged (App. G ). As Table 1 shows, it largely preserves the teacher’s performance at a smaller size and lower latency.

sections.heading: Human preference study.
sections.text: Our perceptual claim rests on automatic metrics, so we test it directly with human observers. Each trial shows the degraded input and the ground truth above two anonymous restorations and asks which repair is better, judging both match to the real scene and how good the image looks. The participants can also choose undecided. The four baselines are Real-HAT-GAN, DiffBIR, SUPIR, and TSD-SR. The pool is 100 100 images, 25 25 drawn uniformly at random from each benchmark with a fixed seed. Method identity is never shown and left/right assignment is randomised (App. A gives the full protocol). Human observers prefer RAESR to every baseline (Table 2 ), including a weak win over TSD-SR.

sections.heading: 5 Analysis
sections.text: This section tests the central hypothesis of the paper, that RAESR’s performance comes from the substrate, which embeds degraded images near the manifold and guides the mapping at every level, rather than from the decoder. Protocols and full tables are in Apps. D , E and H .

sections.heading: 5.1 Degraded images are embedded near the manifold
sections.text: Figure 6: Raw metric curves along the latent line z α = ( 1 − α ) ​ z LR + α ​ z HR z_{\alpha}=(1-\alpha)\,z_{\mathrm{LR}}+\alpha\,z_{\mathrm{HR}} , decoded at eleven points. Curves are means over 2,000 2{,}000 images. For 2,000 2{,}000 images in the LSDIR dataset, we apply the same level of degradation as in the training, embed the degraded and clean images, and decode the latent line z α = ( 1 − α ) ​ z LR + α ​ z HR z_{\alpha}=(1-\alpha)\,z_{\mathrm{LR}}+\alpha\,z_{\mathrm{HR}} at eleven evenly distributed points. Two latent spaces are compared: the fused DINOv3-L latent with the RAEv2 decoder finetuned for clean-image reconstruction at 512 2 512^{2} and the SD3 VAE. We evaluate four metrics, LPIPS, DISTS, NIQE and MANIQA, on the decoded images at those eleven points along the latent line and then averaged them across all images. The comparison is endpoint-matched. Fig. 6 shows a consistent picture. On all four metrics, the line in the fused latent recovers the statistics of the clean image much faster than in the VAE latent, and the two curves separate most widely in the middle. The degraded image is therefore encoded relatively closer both to the manifold and to the embedding of the faithful high-resolution image. The fused latent embeds the degraded image near the manifold, so a short move along the return path already restores naturalness and sharpness. sections.heading: 5.2 The decoder relies on every level of the substrate
sections.text: Each level of information in the substrate is essential to guiding the map to the correct embedding on the manifold, and the decoder relies on all of them. With every weight frozen, we replace one band of the average with its training-set mean tokens, and re-score the released model: the shallowest eight layers, the deepest eight, and additionally the broadcast term (Fig. 7 ). Removing the shallow band severely deteriorates the fidelity metrics , while the perceptual metrics deteriorate only slightly. Removing the deep band does the opposite. Removing the broadcast term as well widens both effects. We also randomly remove 8 layers and the deterioration shows no trend (App. E ). The sample images on the right show two distinct failure modes. Without the shallow band the output loses fidelity to the input. The color balance and the contrast shift, and structure is synthesised without reference to the observed pixels. Without the deep semantics-rich band, the decoder cannot determine what to synthesise, and it selects the safest option, a plausible generic texture. sections.heading: 5.3 The semantics come from the substrate, not the decoder
sections.text: The remaining attribution question is whether the result belongs to the representation or to the 415 415 M decoder and its recipe. It is reasonable to suspect that the decoder could ignore the semantics in the latent and learn its own from the pixel record. We keep everything and only replace the frozen DINOv3-L with the frozen SD3 VAE ( Esser et al., 2024 ) . The decoder, its initialisation and the three-stage recipe are unchanged up to minor deviations (App. H ). The VAE substrate loses on all nine metrics (table in Fig. 8 ). Under heavy degradation the model either paints confident, sharp, wrong content or does not produce a clean, natural image at all, because the degraded image is encoded too far from the manifold and the substrate provides too little direct semantic guidance.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.text: Real-world SR is the task of mapping a degraded image back onto the manifold of clean, sharp and natural images, and to the point on it that is faithful to the input. Which latent space the mapping is performed in therefore decides how hard the task is. A suitable substrate embeds degraded images near the manifold, so the map back is short, and carries information at every level, from the pixel record to semantics, so the map is guided to the faithful point. The fused layers of a frozen DINOv3-L are such a space. With only one decoder pass, our RAESR attains the best fidelity–perception and efficiency–perception trade-offs among the twelve published methods we evaluate. Human observers prefer its restorations to those of four competitive models we evaluated. We therefore argue that the choice of substrate deserves more attention than the SR literature currently gives.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: RAESR has two limitations. Its restorations are produced in one pass with no mechanism for trading compute for quality, so unlike the multi-step methods it cannot spend more steps on a hard image. Our claim about what makes a substrate suitable is supported on one encoder family. We characterise the fused layers of DINOv3-L and test a single alternative substrate (§ 5.3 ), leaving open how other representation encoders behave.

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: Each trial shows the degraded input and the ground truth, labelled in plain words, above two anonymous restorations, and asks which repair is better, judging together whether the output matches the real scene, with nothing invented or changed, and whether it looks sharp and natural. A third option records a tie. Showing the ground truth is deliberate: it makes the study measure faithfulness and quality together, which is the claim of the paper, rather than realism alone. The pool is 100 100 images, 25 25 drawn uniformly at random from each benchmark’s evaluation set with a fixed seed and no author selection at any stage, restored by the same official checkpoints and defaults as Table 1 and served at native 512 × 512 512{\times}512 with tap-to-zoom. Method identity is never shown, left/right assignment is randomised per trial, trial order is shuffled per participant, and each participant judges 25 25 distinct images so no scene is seen twice within a session.

sections.heading: Quality control.
sections.text: Three catch trials per participant, mixed invisibly into the sequence, compare RAESR against the bicubically upsampled input; a participant failing more than one is excluded entirely, as is one whose median response time falls under 3 3 s. Both rules were fixed before collection. The preference rate is RAESR votes over the sum of RAESR and baseline votes, with ties excluded and reported in Table 2 .

sections.heading: B.4 The fused perceptual score of Figure 2
sections.text: The vertical axis of Figure 2 fuses the six perceptual columns of Table 1 (DISTS, NIQE, MUSIQ, MANIQA, TOPIQ, CLIP-IQA) into one number per method. DISTS and NIQE are negated so that higher is better on all six. Each metric is then min–max normalised over the 14 14 rows, s i , m = v i , m − min j ⁡ v j , m max j ⁡ v j , m − min j ⁡ v j , m , s_{i,m}\;=\;\frac{v_{i,m}-\min_{j}v_{j,m}}{\max_{j}v_{j,m}-\min_{j}v_{j,m}}, (6) and the fused score of method i i is the unweighted mean 1 6 ​ ∑ m s i , m \frac{1}{6}\sum_{m}s_{i,m} . It lowers the dimension of the shallow layers ( 28 → 19 28\rightarrow 19 components at layer 7 7 ) and raises it for the deep layers ( 285 → 326 285\rightarrow 326 at layer 19 19 ), and recovery moves the same way, up for the shallow layers and down for the deep ones.

sections.heading: Noise augmentation is not the mechanism.
sections.text: The RAE decoder is trained on noise-smoothed latents ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Singh et al., 2026 ) , so its early naturalness could be suspected to come from this trained robustness. Robustness is an invariance. Under a perturbation it keeps the decode what it already was, which is exactly the behaviour of the random walk above; the true line instead changes the decode toward the clean image, and an invariance cannot produce an improvement. The robustness is also direction-blind, so it cannot explain why one specific direction, toward z HR z_{\mathrm{HR}} , improves every metric family at once (Fig. 6 ).

sections.heading: Wrong-target control: membership is not fidelity.
sections.text: A second control interpolates z LR z_{\mathrm{LR}} toward the clean embedding of a different image (a fixed derangement of the manifest). Both decoders decode this wrong line to fully natural images (NIQE 3.3 3.3 – 3.4 3.4 and MUSIQ ≈ 72 {\approx}72 at α = 1 \alpha{=}1 ) while LPIPS to the true image never falls below 0.74 0.74 . Reaching the manifold and reaching the right point on it are separate quantities, which is why Fig. 6 reports one metric for each; it is also the geometric form of the hallucination failure: a restorer can land on the manifold at the wrong point.

sections.heading: Appendix F The adversarial term: schedule
sections.text: § 3.4 describes the critic; this appendix gives its schedule. Stage 2 runs the critic on the full 512 512 px image with one update per generator step. Three scheduling choices in the final stage matter more than the loss weights. (i) The critic sees a 496 × 496 496{\times}496 centre crop while every other loss sees the full 512 512 px image, so that DINOv3-B’s 16 16 px patch grid is offset by half a patch from the decoder’s 16 16 px token grid. The decoder produces each 16 16 px patch from one token, which can leave faint seams on the patch borders. If the two grids coincided, every seam would lie on a critic patch border, at the same position in every patch, and the critic would learn it as part of a real image. With the offset, each seam runs through the middle of a critic patch, where the critic detects it and pushes the decoder to remove it. (ii) The critic runs on a two-time-scale update rule ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) (a 6 × 6\times higher learning rate and two updates per generator step), since a frozen-feature critic that lags the generator supplies no usable gradient. (iii) The adversarial term is gated: the critic is warmed at λ adv = 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{adv}}\!=\!0 and the weight then ramped in linearly, so the decoder settles on reconstruction before the critic engages.

Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley Affiliation: Alibaba Group Email: wanzhoulei@berkeley.edu Cuifeng Shen Affiliation: Alibaba Group Yanjin He Affiliation: University of Michigan, Ann Arbor Maohua Li Affiliation: Nanjing University Hua Yuan Affiliation: Southeast University Per-Olof Persson Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley Hanlin Tang Affiliation: Alibaba Group Abstract In an image latent space, the embeddings of high-resolution, natural, and sharp images form a manifold. Degradation of high-resolution images pushes their embeddings off this manifold. Real-world super-resolution (SR) then becomes the task of mapping the degraded embedding back onto this manifold: not anywhere on the manifold, but to the point that preserves what the input still carries, both its semantics and pixel details. Every published method implements this mapping in a reconstruction-oriented latent space or pixel space. We claim these spaces are the wrong substrates for SR. Low-resolution and degraded images are embedded far from the manifold, making the mapping difficult and expensive. The lack of semantic information in these substrates also makes it difficult to navigate to the faithful point on the manifold, causing severe hallucination when degradation is heavy. Thus, restoring in a suitable latent space is crucial to the SR task. We show that the latent space of 23 23 fused layers of a frozen DINOv3-L is one such space that makes the SR task easier. Degraded images are embedded near the manifold. Moreover, this substrate contains a hierarchy of information, from pixel record to degradation-robust semantics, directly guiding the model to find the faithful point on the manifold. On this substrate, a 415 415 M decoder is trained under reconstruction and adversarial objectives to map the degraded embeddings back and decode to pixel space in one pass. The resulting model, RAESR, attains the best fidelity–perception trade-off among state-of-the-art adversarial and diffusion-based restorers on RealSR, DRealSR, LSDIR and DIV2K-Val, at 37 37 ms per 512 × 512 512{\times}512 image on a single H20 GPU. Swapping the substrate for a VAE latent under an identical recipe loses on every metric. 1 Introduction In an image latent space, the embeddings of clean, sharp, natural images form a manifold. Degradation pushes an image’s embedding off this manifold, and real-world SR is the task of mapping it back onto the correct point on the manifold, the point that stays faithful to the input in both semantics and surviving detail. Choosing the suitable latent space as the substrate for this task is therefore crucial. A suitable space should offer two properties. First, degraded images should be embedded near the manifold, so that the map back is easier and cheaper. Second, the space should carry a rich hierarchy of information to directly guide the map to the faithful point. High-level semantics tell the model which details are correct to synthesise, and low-level pixel information tells it which details must be preserved and what is noise to be removed. Current real-world SR methods restore in spaces with neither property. They either restore in the pixel space itself ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) , or in the latent of a variational autoencoder ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Wu et al., 2024b ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024a ) . Since these spaces are reconstruction-oriented, they faithfully preserve the degradation. As a result, degraded images are embedded far from the manifold (Fig. 1 a). The map to the manifold is therefore hard and expensive by default, and the lack of semantic information makes it even harder to navigate to the faithful point on the manifold. Lightweight GAN restorers in these spaces usually miss the manifold. Other methods make the distant map possible by training or adopting a visual generative prior such as diffusion, and pay with huge model size and slow inference. Even then, the long and weakly guided map can land on the manifold away from the faithful point, creating hallucinations (Fig. 1 a). Mitigations have been tried: fine-tuning the encoder to close the distance between degraded and clean embeddings ( Chen et al., 2025b ) , and injecting extra semantic guidance, from a text encoder ( Wu et al., 2024b ; Yu et al., 2024 ) or from the features of a vision foundation model ( Wu et al., 2026 ; Jangid et al., 2025 ) . However, these never solve the problem itself. We believe SR must be conducted in a suitable latent space to be efficient, and we claim that the averaged layers of the DINOv3-L encoder form such a latent space (§ 3.1 ). DINOv3 ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) is a self-supervised vision transformer trained on 1.7 1.7 billion curated, unlabelled images by self-distillation. Its network learns to match its own representations across augmented views of the same image, rather than to reconstruct pixels. As a result, degraded images are encoded close to the manifold (Fig. 1 b). The decoded images along the straight interpolation line between the degraded and the clean embedding show this directly (Fig. 1 , strips). In this latent space the decodes turn clear and natural much earlier than in the SD3-VAE latent (§ 5.1 ). Moreover, the fusion preserves a hierarchy of information, from a near-lossless pixel record in the shallow layers to degradation-robust semantics in the deep layers, which provides direct guidance for the map to the faithful point (§ 3.1 ). Therefore, the one-step map is much easier to learn, as shown in Fig. 1 b. Figure 1: The choice of latent space decides the task. (a) A reconstruction-oriented latent. (b) The fused DINOv3-L latent (ours). Strips: decoded images along the straight latent line z α = ( 1 − α ) ​ z LR + α ​ z HR z_{\alpha}=(1-\alpha)\,z_{\mathrm{LR}}+\alpha\,z_{\mathrm{HR}} in each space. RAESR is built on this substrate. One pass of this single trained 415 415 M decoder maps the degraded embedding back and decodes it to pixels. Averaged over four benchmarks, RAESR is first among the twelve published methods we evaluate on NIQE, MANIQA and DISTS and second on MUSIQ, LPIPS and TOPIQ (Table 1 ). It attains the best fidelity–perception trade-off and the best efficiency–perception trade-off (Fig. 2 ), at 719 719 M inference parameters and 37 37 ms per image on one H20. The vertical axis fuses the six perceptual metrics, each min–max normalized and re-oriented, then averaged with equal weight. (a) against LPIPS; (b) against measured latency (one H20, batch 1 1 ). Construction and robustness checks of the fused score: App. B.4 . Contributions. (i) We build RAESR, an efficient one-pass restorer that attains the state-of-the-art fidelity–perception and efficiency–perception trade-offs among the twelve published methods we evaluate, at 37 37 ms per image, with a distilled variant at 30 30 ms (§ 4 , App. G ). (ii) We redirect future SR research toward choosing a suitable latent substrate for the task. (iii) We characterize what makes a substrate suitable. Degraded images should be embedded near the manifold. All levels of information should be present in the substrate as direct guidance to the faithful point (§ 1 ). (iv) We rigorously analyze why the fused latent of DINOv3-L is such a space (§ 3.1 , § 5 ). 2 Related Work Restoring in a reconstruction-oriented space. Every line of real-world SR operates in such a space. Since these spaces offer neither of the two aforementioned properties, each family pays its own price. The one-pass adversarial restorers Real-ESRGAN ( Wang et al., 2021 ) , BSRGAN ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) and Real-HAT-GAN ( Chen et al., 2023 ) perform the map directly in one step, with no generative prior or external guidance. They are small and fast, but they fall short of the manifold and outputs are blurry. The diffusion line makes the long map feasible with a pretrained text-to-image prior. StableSR ( Wang et al., 2024a ) , DiffBIR ( Lin et al., 2024 ) , SeeSR ( Wu et al., 2024b ) , PASD ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , SUPIR ( Yu et al., 2024 ) and DiT4SR ( Duan et al., 2025 ) sample it over tens of steps, at billions of parameters and seconds per image (Table 1 ). There have also been attempts to mitigate the two defects of the reconstruction-oriented latent space. Against the distance, FaithDiff ( Chen et al., 2025b ) fine-tunes the VAE encoder jointly with the prior to close the gap between degraded and clean latents. DiffBIR ( Lin et al., 2024 ) restores in pixel space before generating. Against the missing direct guidance, StableSR ( Wang et al., 2024a ) trains a time-aware encoder to condition the frozen prior, SeeSR ( Wu et al., 2024b ) conditions on tags from a degradation-aware extractor, PASD ( Yang et al., 2024 ) adds a captioner and pixel-aware cross-attention, SUPIR ( Yu et al., 2024 ) scales to large-scale text annotation, and, nearest to this work, VOSR ( Wu et al., 2026 ) and F2IDiff ( Jangid et al., 2025 ) condition the generator on DINOv2 features. Thus, we need a critic that can provide rich and direct guidance. It needs the same hierarchy of information to decide whether a synthesised region is right for the image at each level, from low-level texture statistics to high-level semantics. Following the projected discriminators of Sauer et al. (2021) and the off-the-shelf critics of Kumari et al. (2022) , we therefore build it on the same representation family the substrate is built from (Fig. 4 ). The restored image and its ground truth pass through a frozen DINOv3-B encoder, and each of its 12 12 layers is read by its own trainable convolutional head, which emits one logit per token as the “realness” of that token in that particular information level. The heads carry 191 191 M learnable parameters in total and are discarded after training. Reading every layer through its own head is the critic-side counterpart of fusing every layer into z z . Realism is judged at every level, from texture statistics to the plausibility of semantics. Two properties of this design, both visible in Fig. 4 , make that realism requirement fine-grained and relative. First, the judgment is dense . No logit is pooled into an image-level score, so every region is judged on its own and a weak region cannot be averaged away by the rest. Second, it is paired by position . The logit of the restoration at position p p is compared with the logit of the ground truth at the same position of the same image, never with a batch statistic. The bar at each position is therefore the realism the reference itself attains there. Where the reference is smooth the bar is low, so the term does not ask for texture the scene does not have. Following the perception–distortion framework of Blau & Michaeli (2018) , we divide the nine metrics into two families. PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS are fidelity metrics and measure the discrepancy between the output and its reference. DISTS, NIQE, MUSIQ, MANIQA, TOPIQ and CLIP-IQA are perceptual metrics and rate the perceived quality of the output as an image in its own right. Within the fidelity family we place the most weight on LPIPS, which is calibrated on human judgments of which of two images is closer to the reference ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) . PSNR and SSIM instead reward exact pixel agreement, and the degradation has made exact agreement impossible. The estimator that maximises PSNR is the blurred posterior mean rather than any sharp image ( Blau & Michaeli, 2018 ; Ledig et al., 2017 ) . Under heavy degradation the model either paints confident, sharp, wrong content or does not produce a clean, natural image at all, because the degraded image is encoded too far from the manifold and the substrate provides too little direct semantic guidance. 6 Conclusion and Limitations Real-world SR is the task of mapping a degraded image back onto the manifold of clean, sharp and natural images, and to the point on it that is faithful to the input. Which latent space the mapping is performed in therefore decides how hard the task is. A suitable substrate embeds degraded images near the manifold, so the map back is short, and carries information at every level, from the pixel record to semantics, so the map is guided to the faithful point. The fused layers of a frozen DINOv3-L are such a space. With only one decoder pass, our RAESR attains the best fidelity–perception and efficiency–perception trade-offs among the twelve published methods we evaluate. Human observers prefer its restorations to those of four competitive models we evaluated. We therefore argue that the choice of substrate deserves more attention than the SR literature currently gives. Limitations. RAESR has two limitations. Its restorations are produced in one pass with no mechanism for trading compute for quality, so unlike the multi-step methods it cannot spend more steps on a hard image. Our claim about what makes a substrate suitable is supported on one encoder family. We characterise the fused layers of DINOv3-L and test a single alternative substrate (§ 5.3 ), leaving open how other representation encoders behave.
